summary: This standards-track document defines DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 options that give a client its coordinate-based location: latitude, longitude, and altitude, with resolution indicators and the reference datum. A network can tell a device where it is as part of normal address setup.

plainLanguage.summary:
When a device joins a network, a DHCP server hands out its address and its settings. This RFC adds two more settings: where the device is, as a latitude, a longitude and a height, and how sure the server is about those numbers.

Two of the options state the uncertainty as a margin around the position, and a third counts how many bits of the numbers are actually meaningful. All three say which reference system the coordinates are measured against, so that two different networks can still be compared.

subtitle: How a DHCP server hands a client its latitude, longitude and altitude, with a stated margin of error.

tldr.problem: Emergency telephony needs to know where a caller is, and a device's network connection already tells the network operator roughly where it is. There was no standard way for a DHCP server to pass that location to the device itself.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines three DHCP options that carry latitude, longitude and altitude, each with either a resolution count of valid bits or an uncertainty value, plus a field naming the coordinate datum the numbers are measured against.
tldr.outcome: A client learns its own coordinates as part of ordinary address configuration, and the numbers stay on the device rather than in a database somewhere. The RFC obsoletes RFC 3825 and also defines conversions to and from the PIDF-LO location format.

facts.label: Latitude and longitude encoding
facts.value: 34-bit fixed point, 9 integer bits and 25 fractional bits

facts.label: Altitude encoding
facts.value: 30-bit fixed point, 22 integer bits and 8 fractional bits

today: RFC 6225 is a Proposed Standard from July 2011. It obsoletes RFC 3825 and has not itself been obsoleted or updated. It defines the DHCPv6 GeoLoc Option 63 and the DHCPv4 GeoLoc Option 144, and keeps the DHCPv4 GeoConf Option 123 from the document it replaces.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The physical location of a network device has a range of applications. In particular, emergency telephony applications rely on knowing the location of a caller in order to determine the correct emergency center.

The location of a device can be represented either in terms of geospatial, or geodetic, coordinates, or as a civic address. Different applications may be more suited to one form of location information, so both the geodetic and civic forms may be used simultaneously. This document specifies DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 options for the coordinate-based geographic location of the client, to be provided by the server; RFC 4776 specifies DHCP options for civic addresses.

A DHCP server can work out where a client is. For example, a wired Ethernet host might use these options for location determination, in which case the location information could be derived from a wiremap by the DHCP server, using the Circuit ID Relay Agent Information Option. The DHCP server could correlate the Circuit ID with the geographic location where the identified circuit terminates, such as the location of the wall jack.

The mechanism may also be used to provide location to wireless hosts. Relay agent sub-options provide one method a DHCP server might use to perform host location determination, but currently they do not include the data sets required for device-level location determination of wireless hosts. In cases where the server uses them, a wireless host can use this mechanism to discover the location of the radio access point, or the area of coverage for the radio access point.

An important feature of this specification is that after the relevant DHCP exchanges have taken place, the location information is stored on the end device rather than somewhere else, where retrieving it might be difficult in practice.
sections.plainLanguage: The network usually knows roughly where a device is, because it knows which cable or which radio it is on. This RFC is about passing that knowledge on to the device, so the device itself can tell an emergency service where it is.

sections.title: Resolution and Uncertainty
sections.content:
The options include fields quantifying the resolution or uncertainty associated with a target location. The RFC states that no inferences relating to privacy policies can be drawn from either uncertainty or resolution values.

Resolution refers to the accuracy of a reported location, as expressed by the number of valid bits in each of the Latitude, Longitude and Altitude fields. The resolution sub-fields exist so that the precision of a reported location can be adjusted easily. Contents beyond the claimed resolution may be randomized to obscure greater precision that might be available.

Uncertainty, in the context of location technology, is a quantification of errors. Any method for determining location is subject to some sources of error. Uncertainty might be the coverage area of a wireless transmitter, the extent of a building, or a single room. It is usually represented as an area within which the target is located, and each of the three axes can be assigned an uncertainty value, which in effect describes a rectangular prism that may be used as a coarse representation of a more complex shape fitting within it.

When representing locations from sources that can quantify uncertainty, the goal is to find the smallest possible rectangular prism that the format can describe, by taking the minimum and maximum values on each axis and making sure the final encoding covers those points. This increases the region of uncertainty but ensures that the region described encompasses the target location.

The Presence Information Data Format Location Object, PIDF-LO, is used to convey location and the associated uncertainty within an emergency call, so a mechanism is needed to convert the DHCP options to PIDF-LO and back. Conversion to PIDF-LO does not increase uncertainty. Conversion from PIDF-LO to the DHCPv4 GeoLoc Option 144 and the DHCPv6 GeoLoc Option 63 increases uncertainty by less than a factor of 2 in each dimension. Since it is not possible to translate an arbitrary PIDF-LO into the DHCP GeoConf Option 123 with a bounded increase in uncertainty, that conversion is not specified.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways of saying how good a position is. One counts how many bits of the numbers are real, so the sender can round the rest off. The other says how big an area the device might be in. Both describe the same idea in different forms, and both are needed for different sources of position.

sections.title: The Three DHCP Options
sections.content:
The options defined here use a similar format, differing primarily in the option code. The DHCPv6 GeoLoc Option has an option code of 63 and holds an option length of 16 for version 1, a latitude uncertainty, a 34-bit latitude, a longitude uncertainty, a 34-bit longitude, an altitude type, an altitude uncertainty, a 30-bit altitude, a 2-bit version field, 3 reserved bits and a 3-bit datum field. The Ver field is always located at the same offset from the beginning of the option, regardless of the version in use. DHCPv6 clients implementing this specification must support receiving version 1 responses, and DHCPv6 servers must send version 1 responses.

The DHCPv4 GeoConf Option has an option code of 123 and an option length of 16. It carries the same coordinates, but the precision fields are resolution counts: LaRes for latitude, LoRes for longitude and AltRes for altitude. Its reserved field is 5 bits rather than 3.

The DHCPv4 GeoLoc Option has an option code of 144 and, for version 1, an option length of 16. It carries the same coordinates and the same uncertainty fields as the DHCPv6 option.

DHCPv4 clients must support receiving the GeoLoc Option 144 version 1, and may support receiving the GeoConf Option 123. Clients request the server to send them by including the option codes in the Parameter Request List option. When a client does not understand a datum value, it must assume the World Geodetic System 1984 datum and proceed accordingly, so that some, perhaps less accurate, location is available. DHCPv4 servers must support sending GeoLoc Option 144 version 1 and should support sending GeoConf Option 123, and a server that provides location information should honour the Parameter Request List in deciding which to send.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three options. One is for DHCPv6 and two are for the older DHCPv4. They carry the same three numbers, and differ in whether they say how big the error is or how many bits of the numbers are trustworthy.

sections.title: Latitude and Longitude Fields
sections.content:
Latitude and longitude are encoded as 34-bit, two's complement, fixed-point values with 9 integer bits and 25 fractional bits. The exact meaning of the values is determined by the datum, and the document uses the same definition for all datums it specifies. When encoding, values are rounded to the nearest 34-bit binary representation, and that imprecision is ignored when decoding.

Positive latitudes are north of the equator and negative latitudes are south. Positive longitudes are east of the Prime Meridian and negative longitudes are west of it. Within the coordinate reference systems defined in the document, longitude values outside the range of -180 to 180 decimal degrees or latitude values outside the range of -90 to 90 degrees must be considered invalid. Server implementations should prevent the entry of invalid values, and consumers must ignore invalid location coordinates and should log errors related to them.

In the GeoConf Option 123, the LaRes value encodes the number of high-order latitude bits that must be considered valid. Any bits entered to the right of this limit must not be considered valid and might be purposely false, or zeroed by the sender. A value of 2 indicates a precision of no greater than one sixth of the globe, and a value of 34 indicates a precision of about 3.11 mm in latitude at the equator. The LoRes value works the same way for longitude, where a value of 34 indicates a precision of about 2.42 mm at the equator; because lines of longitude converge at the poles, the distance is smaller for locations away from the equator.

In the GeoLoc options the uncertainty fields quantify the amount of uncertainty in each value. A value of 0 is reserved to indicate that the uncertainty is unknown, and values greater than 34 are reserved. A point within the region of uncertainty is selected to be the encoded point, and the centroid of the region is often an appropriate choice. The value for uncertainty is the distance from the selected point to the furthest extreme of the region on that axis. The amount of uncertainty is 2 to the power of 8 minus the encoded value, expressed in degrees.
sections.plainLanguage: Latitude and longitude are packed into 34 bits each, with room for whole degrees and a very small fraction of a degree. How many of those bits are meaningful is stated separately, so the sender can round the position off to the accuracy it really has.

sections.title: Altitude
sections.content:
How the altitude value is interpreted depends on the Altitude Type value and the selected datum. Three Altitude Type values are defined: unknown, zero; meters, one; and floors, two.

An Altitude Type of zero indicates that the altitude is not given to the client, and the Altitude and Altitude Uncertainty fields can contain any value and must be ignored. A value of one means the altitude is measured in meters, in relation to the zero set by the vertical datum, as a 30-bit fixed-point two's complement integer with 22 integer bits and 8 fractional bits.

A value of two means the altitude is measured in floors. Since altitude in meters may not be known within a building, a floor indication may be more useful. It is expressed in the same 30-bit fixed-point form, and is relative to the ground level of the building; floors below ground level are negative. Non-integer values can represent intermediate floors such as mezzanines, so a mezzanine between floor 1 and floor 2 could be 1.25, and mezzanines between floors 4 and 5 could be 4.5 and 4.75.

In the GeoConf Option 123, the AltRes value encodes the number of high-order altitude bits that should be considered valid, and values above 30 are undefined and reserved. An AltRes value of 0 indicates an unknown altitude and the most precise altitude would have a value of 30. In the GeoLoc options the AltUnc value quantifies the amount of uncertainty in the altitude, in the same units as the altitude, with a value of 0 reserved to indicate that the uncertainty is not known and values above 30 reserved. Altitude uncertainty only applies to Altitude Type 1.
sections.plainLanguage: The height field comes with a label saying how to read it. It can be metres above the vertical datum, a floor number within a building, or simply unknown. A floor number can be fractional, so a mezzanine between floors can be given exactly.

sections.title: Coordinate Datum
sections.content:
The Datum field determines how coordinates are organized and related to the real world. Three datums are defined, based on the definitions of the International Association of Oil and Gas Producers.

Datum 1 is WGS84, the World Geodetic System 1984 coordinate reference system, identified by the EPSG code 4979 with altitude or 4326 without. Datum 2 combines NAD83, the North American Datum 1983, for the horizontal latitude and longitude values with the North American Vertical Datum of 1988 for the vertical. It is used for referencing location on land, not near tidal water, within North America; NAD83 is identified by the EPSG code 4269 and NAVD88 by 5703. Datum 3 combines NAD83 for the horizontal values with Mean Lower Low Water as the vertical datum, and is used for referencing location on or near tidal water within North America.

All hosts must support the WGS84 datum. When a DHCPv4 or DHCPv6 client does not understand a datum value, it must assume WGS84, with the EPSG code 4326 or 4979 depending on whether an altitude value is present, and proceed accordingly. Assuming that a less accurate location value is better than none ensures that some, perhaps less accurate, location is available to the client.
sections.plainLanguage: The same pair of numbers can mean different places on Earth depending on the reference system used. The datum field names that reference system, so a position from one network can be compared with a position from another.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Geopriv requirements, including security requirements, are discussed in RFC 3693, and a threat analysis is provided in RFC 3694.

Since there is no privacy protection for DHCP messages, an eavesdropper who can monitor the link between the DHCP server and the requesting client can discover this location information. To minimize the unintended exposure of location information, the option should be returned by DHCP servers only when the DHCP client has included it in its parameter request list.

Where critical decisions might be based on the value of this option, DHCP authentication as defined in RFC 3118 and RFC 3315 should be used to protect the integrity of the DHCP options. Link-layer confidentiality and integrity protection may also be employed to reduce the risk of location disclosure and tampering.
sections.plainLanguage: DHCP traffic is not private, so anyone watching the link can read the position the server sends. The RFC asks servers to send it only when the client asks for it, and asks for authentication and link-level encryption where a decision depends on the value.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content:
The document defines three registries for IANA to maintain. The Altitude Type registry holds an integer referring to the value used in the three options, with values 0 to 2 assigned and values 3 to 15 unassigned. Each entry carries a description of the altitude and a reference that must define how the 30-bit altitude values and the associated 6-bit uncertainty are interpreted.

The Datum registry holds an integer referring to the value used in the three options. Value 0 is reserved and values 1 to 3 are assigned, with values 4 to 7 unassigned. Each reference must include the specification of both the horizontal and vertical datum and must define how the 34-bit values and the respective 6-bit uncertainties are interpreted.

The GeoLoc Option Version registry holds an integer referring to the version used in the DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 GeoLoc options. Value 0 is reserved, value 1 has been assigned, and values 2 to 3 are unassigned. Each reference must describe the version and specify the parameters for both the DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 GeoLoc options.
sections.plainLanguage: Three lists are created so that later additions can be made without rewriting the document: one for altitude types, one for coordinate datums, and one for the version of the option format.

viz.caption: The 16 octets of option data in the DHCPv6 GeoLoc option, version 1

fields.name: Latitude
fields.desc: A fixed-point value with 9 integer bits and 25 fractional bits.

fields.name: Longitude
fields.desc: A fixed-point value with 9 integer bits and 25 fractional bits.

fields.name: AType
fields.desc: Altitude type: unknown, meters or floors.

fields.name: Altitude
fields.desc: The altitude value, interpreted according to the AType field.

fields.name: Ver
fields.desc: Option version. This specification defines version 1.

fields.name: Datum
fields.desc: The map datum used for the coordinates in this option.

items.label: No known altitude
items.desc: The altitude is not given to the client. The Altitude and Altitude Uncertainty fields can contain any value and must be ignored.

items.label: Altitude in meters
items.desc: Measured in meters, relative to the zero set by the vertical datum. A 30-bit fixed-point value with 22 integer bits and 8 fractional bits.

items.label: Altitude in floors
items.desc: Measured in floors, relative to the ground level of the building. A 30-bit fixed-point value with 22 integer bits and 8 fractional bits.

items.label: Unassigned
items.desc: Not assigned to any altitude type.

items.label: WGS84
items.desc: The World Geodetic System 1984 coordinate reference system, EPSG code 4979 with altitude and 4326 without. Every host must support this datum.

items.label: NAD83 and NAVD88
items.desc: NAD83 for latitude and longitude with the North American Vertical Datum of 1988 for altitude. Used for location on land in North America.

items.label: NAD83 and MLLW
items.desc: NAD83 for latitude and longitude with Mean Lower Low Water as the vertical datum. Used for location on or near tidal water in North America.
